title: Intervals and bit tricks in Java (>>>, TreeMap, int overflow)
seriesDescription: Shortest paths, union-find, tries, intervals, bits, dynamic programming, greedy and backtracking with Java code. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Merge intervals with Arrays.sort, TreeMap calendar booking, CIDR masks, Kernighan popcount, shifts mod 32, >>> and int overflow.
source: Oracle Java Tutorials (bitwise operators); JLS 15.19 (shift operators), 15.17, 4.2.2; Java TreeMap and Integer API docs; LeetCode Merge Intervals, My Calendar I, Missing Number

questions.prompt: Write a Java method `int[][] merge(int[][] iv)` that merges all overlapping closed intervals (touching intervals like [1,2] and [2,3] also merge) and returns the result in sorted order.
questions.explanation: Copy `x` into a new array before adding so you do not mutate the caller's input. Prefer `Integer.compare` over `a[0] - b[0]`, which can overflow with extreme values. Time O(n log n). Other valid approaches exist, e.g. keeping start and end in local variables.

collects results in a list or array and returns it

questions.prompt: Write a Java method `boolean inSubnet(int ip, int network, int prefixLen)` that returns true if the 32-bit IPv4 address ip belongs to the CIDR block `network/prefixLen`, using bit operations. Handle `prefixLen == 0`.
questions.explanation: The guard matters: in Java the shift distance of an `int` shift is taken mod 32 (JLS 15.19), so `-1 << 32` is still -1 and a /0 would wrongly demand an exact match. An alternative is `(ip ^ network) >>> (32 - p) == 0` with the same guard.

questions.prompt: Write a Java method `int popcount(int n)` that counts the set bits of an int using the `n & (n - 1)` trick, without `Integer.bitCount` or `Integer.toBinaryString`.
questions.explanation: Runs in O(number of set bits) and also works for negative ints, which simply have up to 32 set bits. In real code use `Integer.bitCount(n)`, which the JVM can compile to a single instruction.

checks.label: clears the lowest set bit with n & (n - 1)

questions.prompt: Write a Java class `MyCalendar` with `boolean book(int start, int end)` for half-open events [start, end). It returns false (and stores nothing) if the new event overlaps an existing one, else stores it and returns true. Use a `TreeMap<Integer, Integer>` from start to end.
questions.explanation: Only the nearest neighbours can collide, so each booking is O(log n). Half-open intervals let [10,20) and [20,30) coexist. A list scan is O(n) per booking and also valid for small inputs.

checks.label: looks up the previous event with floorKey or floorEntry/lowerKey
looks up the next event with ceilingKey or higherKey
returns false on a collision and true otherwise
stores the new event with put

questions.prompt: Write a Java method `int missingNumber(int[] nums)` for an array holding n distinct numbers taken from 0..n with one missing; return the missing one in O(n) time and O(1) extra space using XOR or a sum.
questions.explanation: XOR of 0..n with every element cancels all pairs and leaves the missing number. The sum version `n(n+1)/2 - sum` needs `long` when n is large, because `n * (n + 1)` overflows int near n = 46,341. Sorting or a hash set would use more time or space.

checks.label: uses the array length as n
combines values with XOR or a sum

questions.prompt: 1000 in binary is 1111101000. What does `Integer.bitCount(1000)` return?
questions.explanation: Ones in 1111101000: five in a row plus one more = 6. Brian Kernighan's `n &= n - 1` loop would iterate exactly 6 times.

questions.prompt: What does the `int` expression `1 << 33` evaluate to in Java?
questions.explanation: For `int` operands only the low 5 bits of the shift distance are used (JLS 15.19), so 33 acts as 33 mod 32 = 1 and the result is `1 << 1` = 2. For a `long` you would write `1L << 33`.

questions.prompt: In Java, what does the `int` expression `100000 * 100001` evaluate to, given that the true product is 10,000,100,000?
questions.explanation: The product exceeds 2^31 - 1, so it wraps modulo 2^32: 10,000,100,000 - 2 * 4,294,967,296 = 1,410,165,408, which fits in an int. Use `100000L * 100001` or `long` variables to avoid it.

questions.prompt: A Java developer writes `if (n & (n - 1) == 0)` to test for a power of two. What happens?
questions.explanation: Always parenthesise: `(n & (n - 1)) == 0`. Precedence from high to low: shifts, relational, equality, then &, ^, |.

options.text: It fails to compile, because == binds tighter than &, giving int & boolean.
options.why: Correct: `n - 1 == 0` is evaluated first, producing a boolean that cannot be ANDed with an int.

options.text: It works as intended, because bitwise operators are evaluated before comparisons.
options.why: In Java == has higher precedence than &, the opposite of what this assumes.

options.text: It compiles and silently tests whether n equals 1.
options.why: It does not compile, so no silent wrong answer is produced.

options.text: It compiles but throws `ArithmeticException` for n = 0.
options.why: No division happens, so `ArithmeticException` cannot arise from this expression.

questions.prompt: You need a mask with bit 40 set, held in a `long`. Which expression is correct?
questions.explanation: In Java an `int` shift uses only 5 bits of the distance, and a `long` shift uses 6 bits. Mix the literal type with the destination type.

options.why: Correct: the long literal makes the shift operate on 64 bits.
The int shift distance is taken mod 32, so this equals `1 << 8` = 256.
Shifting back down by 24 leaves bit 16, not bit 40.
The first int shift is fine, but the second wraps out of the int, leaving 0.

questions.prompt: Consider the Java expression `-1 >>> 28` on an int.
questions.explanation: Use `>>>` to treat an int as unsigned (IP addresses!). `-1 >> 28` stays -1 because `>>` sign-extends.
questions.reason: The `>>>` operator sign-extends the left operand while shifting.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.c: Right: -1 is 32 ones; >>> fills with zeros leaving the top 4 bits as 1111 = 15, and >>> does not sign-extend, so R is false.

questions.explanation: Remember to build the mask with `-1 << (32 - prefixLen)` and guard `prefixLen == 0`.
questions.assertion: `(ip & mask) == (network & mask)` tests whether ip is in the block `network/prefixLen`.
questions.reason: The mask zeroes the host bits, so only the network bits are compared.

whys.a: Right: R describes what the mask does, which is exactly why the comparison works.
whys.b: R is the explanation, not a side fact.

questions.prompt: Sorting intervals in Java with `Arrays.sort(int[][] iv, comparator)`.
questions.explanation: For [1,10] then [2,3], extending with the second end would shrink the interval; max keeps 10.
questions.assertion: `Math.max` is used to extend the end of the last merged interval.
questions.reason: `Arrays.sort` on an object array such as `int[]`[] is a stable sort.

whys.a: Stability of the sort does not explain why max is needed; nested intervals do.
whys.b: Right: both are true, but max handles an interval nested inside another, which has nothing to do with sort stability.

questions.explanation: Narrowing casts keep the low bits, and the top bit then reads as the sign.
questions.reason: A Java byte is a signed 8-bit type with range -128 to 127.

whys.a: A is false, so R cannot explain it.
whys.d: Right: R is true and is exactly why A is false; (byte) 200 is -56. Mask with & 0xFF to read it as 200.

questions.prompt: Match each Java operator or method with what it does.
questions.explanation: Java has both `>>` (arithmetic) and `>>>` (logical) shifts; `n & -n` works through two's complement; XOR with itself cancels; `Integer.bitCount` is the library popcount. `Integer.reverse` is the bit-reversal method.

right.text: Signed right shift that copies the sign bit
Unsigned right shift that fills with zeros

questions.prompt: Complete the recurrence that counts the set bits of every number from 0 to n in O(n) with an `int[] bits`.
questions.explanation: This is LeetCode 338 (Counting Bits). The answer for i reuses an already computed smaller number, so it is a DP over bits; `i & (i - 1)` works too: `bits[i] = bits[i & (i - 1)] + 1`.
questions.text: With bits[0] = {1}, use bits[i] = bits[i {2} 1] + (i {3} 1): drop the lowest bit, then add it back if it was set.
